analysis.one_liner: Speeds up and makes more transparent the approval process Medicare Advantage plans use before covering care.
analysis.headline: The bill won 52 Senate cosponsors from both parties but never received a committee vote or floor action before Congress adjourned.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare Advantage plans are private insurance plans that cover people on Medicare, and they often require doctors to get advance approval — "prior authorization" — before a patient can get a test, treatment, or medical device. This bill would require those plans to use an electronic approval system that gives instant answers for requests that are routinely approved, and to publish statistics each year on how many requests they approve, how long they take, and how often their denials are overturned on appeal. It would also require the government to write rules protecting patients from delays and denials. The bill had 52 Senate cosponsors from both parties but never got a vote in the Senate Finance Committee, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 30 million seniors and disabled people enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans, who would face fewer treatment delays and have public data showing how often their plan denies care. Doctors would also benefit from faster, electronic approvals instead of faxed paperwork.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicare Advantage plans to run an electronic prior authorization system that can instantly approve requests for services that are routinely approved, so patients wait days instead of weeks in common cases.

Requires plans to publish each year how often they approve or deny prior authorization requests, how long decisions take, how often denials are overturned on appeal, and whether artificial-intelligence-style decision tools were used in denials.

Directs HHS to write rules requiring timely decisions, explanations for denials, review by qualified medical personnel, continuity of care when patients switch plans, and appeal information given to the patient when a request is denied.
Requires plans to disclose to patients and providers the criteria they use to decide what care gets approved, except proprietary information.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers, who would have to build electronic approval systems, publicly report their denial and delay rates, and get faster decisions to doctors — costs they could not shift directly to patients. Health insurers generally face new disclosure and compliance work.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves much to HHS rulemaking — the definition of a 'real-time decision,' which services get instant approval, and the beneficiary protection standards — so its practical strength depends on how regulators write the rules.
Plans could keep approval criteria secret from beneficiaries and providers where revealing them would disclose proprietary information, limiting how much the transparency provisions actually expose.
Compliance costs for plans — building electronic systems and publishing annual statistics — could be passed along or used as a reason to narrow plan networks or benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to seniors — faster decisions and fewer wrongful denials of care — are real, though the bill relies on regulation rather than outright limits, so insurers could still deny care under slower, opaque procedures. The costs fall on insurers (compliance and disclosure work) and somewhat on providers (new systems), and stricter approvals could marginally slow plan cost control. On balance the design is modest but sound; the real drawback is that it never happened.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 20, 2021 and read twice, then referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No further action appears in the record: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Despite 52 cosponsors spanning both parties — including senators from both sides of the aisle — the bill never received even a committee vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers keep prior authorization as an unmonitored cost-control tool, and no senior gained the faster approvals the bill promised.

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: Sens. Kyrsten Sinema, John Thune, and Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 52 Senate cosponsors (29 of 48 Democrats, 23 of 50 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it majority-of-Senate support before it stalled.

against.name: Medicare Advantage insurance industry
against.role: Private insurers covering most Medicare beneficiaries
against.what_they_did: Opposed strict prior authorization mandates; insurers' trade associations backed a narrower regulatory approach and the bill never advanced past introduction.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no markup, no vote, no report — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was evenly bipartisan — 29 of 48 Democratic and 23 of 50 Republican senators cosponsored, with the bill introduced by a Republican and originally backed by senators of both parties.

industries.note: The bill would force plans to automate and speed up prior authorization, publicly report denial and delay statistics, and disclose their approval criteria — cutting into a cost-control tool they use to manage spending. It regulates the industry without removing it from Medicare.

industries.industry: Doctors and other health care providers
industries.note: Providers would spend less time chasing faxes and appeals, get decisions faster, and know in advance what documentation each plan requires.
The mandate for standardized electronic prior authorization systems would create demand for certified health IT software to connect providers and plans.
